content: The 2019 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services include a detailed analysis of the cost-effectiveness of using dual HIV/syphilis tests in antenatal care (ANC) settings across countries with varying HIV prevalence. This analysis, published as Web Annex G, explores the potential benefits of dual testing for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV and congenital syphilis. Background: Dual HIV/syphilis testing has been proposed as a strategy to prevent the transmission of HIV and syphilis from mother to child. However, the cost-effectiveness of implementing such dual testing in ANC settings, particularly in countries with differing HIV prevalence rates, remains uncertain. Methods: The study utilized Markov decision-analytic models to estimate the costs and infant health outcomes associated with maternal testing strategies. These outcomes included the number of infections, deaths, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). The strategies compared were: 1. Testing at the first ANC visit using individual tests (base case). 2. Testing at the first ANC visit using a dual HIV/syphilis test. The analysis was conducted in countries with high/intermediate HIV prevalence (South Africa, Kenya) and low HIV prevalence (Colombia, Ukraine). Strategies with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of less than $500 per DALY averted were considered cost-effective. Findings: 1. Cost-Saving Results: Routine testing at the first ANC visit with a dual test was found to be cost-saving compared to individual tests in all four countries: Kenya: ICER = -$23 South Africa: ICER = -$316 Colombia: ICER = -$844 Ukraine: ICER = -$454 2. Cost-Effectiveness of Retesting: Routine retesting with individual tests was cost-effective in Kenya (ICER = $437) and Colombia (ICER = $2,685) when compared to individual testing at the first ANC visit. Interpretation: Incorporating dual HIV/syphilis testing into ANC services can be either cost-effective or cost-saving across countries with varying HIV prevalence. This approach supports the dual elimination of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV and congenital syphilis, aligning with global health goals. WHO Recommendations: The WHO recommends that all pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at least once, ideally during the first ANC visit. This recommendation is particularly strong for syphilis testing (moderate-quality evidence) and HBsAg testing in settings with ≥2% HBsAg seroprevalence (low-quality evidence). Testing Scenarios: 1. Base Case (Individual Tests): Includes rapid HIV tests and laboratory-based syphilis tests (RPR and TPHA for confirmation). 2. Dual Test: A single, point-of-care rapid test for both HIV and syphilis. 3. Late ANC Testing: Conducted between 36 to 39 weeks of gestation. Health Impact and Cost-Effectiveness: The study modeled the total costs, HIV and syphilis infections, DALYs, and incremental costs for each scenario. Dual testing consistently demonstrated cost savings and health benefits compared to individual testing strategies. General Disclaimers: The publication emphasizes that the findings do not imply endorsement of specific products or organizations by WHO. The responsibility for the interpretation and use of the material lies with the reader. WHO is not liable for any damages arising from the use of the information. Conclusion: The findings highlight the potential of dual HIV/syphilis testing to improve maternal and child health outcomes while being cost-effective or cost-saving. This supports the broader implementation of dual testing in ANC settings to achieve the elimination of MTCT of HIV and congenital syphilis.
